steps.title: The problem: how do you get to a target?

content.value:
Imagine you want the robot to face exactly 90 degrees. You could:

1. Set a fixed power and stop when close (open-loop, inaccurate)

2. Constantly adjust power based on how far you are from 90 (closed-loop with feedback)

PID is the most common feedback controller in FTC. It stands for Proportional, Integral, Derivative.

Each term addresses a specific problem.

steps.title: P: Proportional — corrects the present error

content.value:
The P term is proportional to the current error.

If you're 30 degrees from the target, the controller applies power proportional to that 30. As you get closer, the power automatically decreases.

Before P control: the robot overshoots wildly or never reaches the target because power doesn't decrease.

After P control: the robot approaches the target smoothly but may stop short (steady-state error) because at small errors, the corrective power is too small to overcome friction.

Formula: output = kP x error

The I term accumulates error over time.

If the robot is stuck 3 degrees from target, P alone may be too weak to move it. The I term adds up the error each cycle until the accumulated correction is large enough to push through.

Before I control: robot stops a few degrees short and stays there.

After I control: the accumulated error builds up, pushes the robot the final few degrees, then resets.

Danger: if tuned too high, the I term causes overshoot and oscillation because it keeps accumulating during overshoot.

Formula: output += kI x error x deltaTime

The D term resists change. It looks at how fast the error is changing.

When the robot approaches the target quickly, the D term applies a braking force proportional to the approach speed.

Before D control: the robot oscillates back and forth around the target.

After D control: the approach is dampened, reducing overshoot and settling faster.

Danger: D amplifies sensor noise. A noisy gyro makes D behave erratically.

Formula: output = kD x (error - prevError) / deltaTime
